A $16,000 raise is a 22% increase — roughly $11–12k more per year after tax, which is likely the single largest lever available for a house down payment, and it also resets the baseline for every future raise and offer you negotiate. The costs on the other side are small and mostly recoverable: five extra minutes of commute is trivial, and while a supportive manager is genuinely valuable, it's also the most fragile thing on your list — managers leave, get reorganized, or change. Betting $16k a year on one person staying in their seat is a bad trade when you've said financial stability is the priority. Two practical caveats: if you're actively applying for a mortgage in the next few months, talk to a lender first, since underwriters may want to see a few pay stubs from the new job (a lateral move in the same field at higher pay is usually fine, but timing matters), and check that the new offer's total compensation — 401(k) match, health premiums, PTO, bonus structure — doesn't quietly erode the gap. Absent a surprise there, this is a clear move.

Your stated reasoning doesn't match your stated priority. A $16,000 raise is roughly 22% more income for five extra minutes of driving and the same kind of work at a comparable company — if you're saving for a house, that's potentially tens of thousands of dollars of down payment over a couple of years, which is exactly the "financial stability" you say you're optimizing for. "The extra money isn't worth a change" isn't a real argument here; it's the kind of thing people say after they've already committed socially and don't want to look flaky. The honest version of your position would be "a supportive manager is worth more than $16k a year to me" — and that *can* be true, but you should say it out loud and test it, because a good manager can leave or get reorganized at any time, while a higher salary base follows you for the rest of your career. The things that would legitimately change my answer are concrete: the new company is financially shaky, the role is a known meat grinder, you'd lose vesting equity worth more than the gap, or your current employer will counter. Check those, then go. Telling your friends you were staying costs you about ten seconds of mild embarrassment.

On the numbers, this offer is worse than it looks. The $16,000 raise is roughly $11,000–12,000 after tax, while a 90-minute each-way commute adds about 2.5 hours a day — roughly 600 hours a year, the equivalent of fifteen extra work weeks — plus real costs. If you're driving, 100+ miles a day runs to $15,000–20,000 a year in fuel, maintenance, tires, insurance, and depreciation at full IRS rates; even on cheap transit you're looking at a few thousand plus the time. That wipes out the raise and may leave you behind, which directly undercuts the house-saving goal. And since it's similar work at a similar-sized company, you're not buying career acceleration either — you'd be trading a supportive manager (genuinely scarce, and the main thing that protects you in a bad quarter) for a lateral move. The move only makes sense if the role is hybrid or remote two-plus days a week, or if you'd relocate — and if relocation is on the table, compare housing costs there before anything else. Absent that, the better financial play is to stay and use the offer as leverage: a concrete competing number is the strongest case you'll ever have for a raise where you are.

stay

The costs you're weighing against it are real but modest and recoverable: 20 extra minutes of round-trip commuting, and the gamble that a new manager won't be as good as your current one. A supportive manager is genuinely valuable, but it's also the least durable thing about a job — managers leave, reorganize, or change, and you can't bank on that relationship the way you can bank on a higher salary. Before you sign, do the ordinary diligence: confirm the total compensation picture (health premiums, retirement match, bonus, PTO) so the $16k isn't quietly eroded, and check that the company is financially stable, since job loss would hurt your savings plan far more than a smaller raise would. If those check out — and in a same-size company doing similar work, they usually do — take it, and set up an automatic transfer of the difference into your house fund so the raise doesn't dissolve into lifestyle.

A 5% bump probably isn't worth losing a good manager and restarting your tenure clock somewhere new; a 25% bump very likely is, and would get you to a down payment materially faster. Get those numbers side by side before you decide — and note that lenders generally like to see stable employment history, so if the raise is marginal, job-hopping right before a mortgage application is a small additional negative.

You're at the absolute bottom of a posted range that goes $25,000 higher, and the recruiter has already volunteered that there's budget flexibility — that's close to an open invitation to counter. The downside risk is minimal: written offers are essentially never rescinded because a candidate politely asks for more, especially when the ask sits inside the company's own advertised band. Counter in the $112,000–$118,000 range (anchoring high but still within the posted range), and justify it with your market value and scope of the role rather than with personal need. Separately, ask for a decision deadline that lands after next week's interview — framed as wanting to be thoughtful, not as leverage-shopping — since a second process, even without an offer in hand, strengthens your position and costs you nothing to preserve. If they hold firm at $95,000, you can still accept; you'd lose nothing but a few days.

Written offers are very rarely rescinded over a polite, well-framed counter; what actually happens is the company says yes, meets you partway, or says the number is firm, and you accept anyway. Ask for a specific figure in the upper-middle of the range (something like $110,000), anchor it in the role's scope and your relevant experience rather than your needs, and keep the tone warm and clearly enthusiastic about the job. Since the goal is to stop the behavior while staying in the role and keeping a workable relationship with this manager, the most proportionate first step is a direct, low-drama conversation with the manager — privately, not in the moment. Something like: "In the meeting on [date] you said I was too old to learn the new system, and something similar on [date]. I don't think you meant it the way it landed, but it undermines me in front of the team and I need it to stop." Many managers making careless age-related remarks have never been told directly and will correct it immediately. Afterward, send a brief, neutral follow-up email ("Thanks for talking today about the comments in the [date] and [date] meetings") — this keeps the tone collaborative while quietly creating a record that you raised it. Keep your existing documentation, and add any new incidents. If the comments continue after that conversation, or if you notice any change in how you're treated after raising it, that's the point to go to HR — and you'll then have a much stronger case, because you'll be able to show the behavior persisted after the manager was explicitly put on notice. Note the one exception: if you have reason to believe this manager reacts badly to being challenged, skip straight to HR.

But you also don't have to jump to a formal complaint to act. The step that best matches both your goal and your comfort level is a brief, private, non-accusatory conversation with your manager: name the specific comments and dates, say plainly that remarks about your age in front of the team undermine you and you'd like them to stop, and leave it there. Most people who make these comments are being careless rather than malicious and will correct course once it's named directly; if your manager is reasonable, that ends it. Keep your documentation either way, and add a note about this conversation — what you said, when, and how they responded. If the comments continue after you've clearly asked them to stop, that changes the picture substantially, and HR stops being an overreaction and becomes the appropriate next step. You'd also then have a much stronger record: not just two remarks, but a pattern that persisted after a direct request.

Keep it about the comments, not their character; most managers making remarks like this are being careless rather than malicious, and a clear, calm objection from the person affected is often enough. Do this in person or by video if you can, then send a short follow-up email summarizing what you discussed — that gives you a contemporaneous record without turning it into a formal complaint. Add that conversation to the notes you're already keeping. If the comments continue after you've raised it, or if your manager reacts with hostility or your work situation worsens, go to HR and use the discrimination process — you'll be in a stronger position having a documented attempt to resolve it directly, and age is a protected characteristic so retaliation is itself actionable. One exception: if you have reason to think your manager will react punitively, or the pattern is longer and more severe than these two incidents suggest, skip the direct conversation and go straight to HR.

The honest answer is that the right move depends on one thing you know and I don't: what was actually said. If the comments touched on a protected characteristic — race, gender, age, disability, religion, pregnancy, etc. — or were targeted and humiliating rather than clumsy, that changes the calculus: a direct conversation with the person who said it can be unsafe, can muddy the record, and the formal process exists precisely for that category. If instead the remarks were tone-deaf, crude, or careless without that edge, a direct, low-drama conversation with your manager is usually the fastest route to your actual goal — it stops, and you keep working there — and HR stays available if it doesn't work. Two other things would sharpen the answer: whether anyone else witnessed or was affected (a pattern others share points toward HR), and whether your manager has historically responded to feedback without retaliating. So: reread your notes and ask whether the content was discriminatory or just inappropriate. Keep the dates and verbatim quotes either way; that documentation is useful under both paths. If after that test it lands in the discrimination bucket, go to HR; if not, raise it directly, be specific about the two incidents, and state plainly what you want to stop.

The counteroffer solves a problem you didn't have. You weren't leaving over pay — you were leaving because you've spent four months without substantive work, and the offer leaves your assignment exactly as it is. Taking it would mean accepting more money to keep doing nothing, which tends to compound the damage: skills atrophy, your résumé develops a gap that's hard to explain, and you lose credibility if you resign again in six months. It also signals to your employer that the staffing problem can be solved with cash rather than real reassignment. The one thing that could legitimately change the calculus is if your current employer put a concrete, specific role on the table — a named project, a start date, a manager — but a salary match alone isn't that. Do some basic diligence on the new role to confirm the work there is actually substantive and the team is funded, then go. If your current employer genuinely values you, let them counter with work, not just money — and if they can't do that in the time you have, that itself answers the question.
